topic: The Bridge Between Change and Accumulation: The Relationship Between Integrals and Derivatives
target_audience: First-year university students or advanced high school students

sections.title: The Hook: The Cheetah's Dash (0:00 - 0:45)
sections.content: Introduce the two main branches of calculus through a physical scenario. Differentiation measures 'instantaneous change' (speedometer), while Integration measures 'total accumulation' (odometer). This section sets the stage for why we need to connect them.
sections.example: An animated Cheetah accelerates across the screen. Above it, a graph shows its velocity. We pose the question: If we know the Cheetah's velocity at every second (Derivative), can we figure out the total distance it traveled (Integral) without adding up infinite tiny steps?

sections.title: Prerequisite Refresh: Slopes and Slices (0:45 - 1:30)
sections.content: Briefly visualize the two operations independently. Differentiation as finding the slope of a tangent line; Integration as calculating the area under a curve using Riemann sums (thin rectangles).
sections.example: A split-screen animation. On the left, a magnifying glass zooms into a curve to show a straight-line slope (dy/dx). On the right, a curve is filled with increasingly thin vertical bars to represent the area.

sections.title: The Accumulation Function (1:30 - 2:30)
sections.content: Introduce the 'Area Function' A(x), which represents the area under a curve f(t) from a fixed point 'a' to a moving point 'x'. This is the 'bridge' concept. Explain that as 'x' moves, the area grows.
sections.example: A 'Scanning Bar' moves from left to right across a graph of f(t). As it moves, the region behind it is shaded, and a new graph A(x) is plotted simultaneously above it, showing the total shaded area growing over time.

sections.title: FTC Part 1: The Rate of Growth (2:30 - 3:30)
sections.content: Demonstrate the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part 1. Show that the rate at which the area A(x) increases is exactly equal to the height of the function f(x) at that point. This proves that the derivative of an integral is the original function.
sections.example: Zoom into the edge of the scanning bar. Show a tiny increase in width (dx). The tiny increase in area (dA) is a rectangle of height f(x) and width dx. Visually demonstrate dA/dx = f(x) using a 'puzzle piece' metaphor where the height of the curve determines the speed of area growth.

sections.title: FTC Part 2: The Shortcut (3:30 - 4:30)
sections.content: Explain the Evaluation Theorem. If Integration and Differentiation are inverses, we can calculate the area under f(x) simply by finding its antiderivative F(x) and calculating F(b) - F(a). No more infinite sums needed.
sections.example: A 'Climb the Ladder' metaphor. To find the area under a velocity curve (f), we simply look at the height difference on the position ladder (F). The animation shows the area under a curve being 'poured' into a vertical cylinder to measure its height difference.

sections.title: Summary: The Symmetry of Calculus (4:30 - 5:00)
sections.content: Conclude by emphasizing the perfect symmetry. Differentiation 'breaks down' a function into its rates; Integration 'builds up' those rates into a total value. They are two sides of the same coin.
sections.example: A circular infographic showing a function f(x). An arrow pointing clockwise (differentiation) leads to f'(x), and an arrow pointing counter-clockwise (integration) leads back to f(x), forming a continuous loop of mathematical logic.
